gen-gf-phudu-gf-ojuju: Ojuju reads friendly and current, its round letters flexing just slightly like springy wire. Phudu works best up big and brief, where its unbroken, uniform line weight can show off without crowding.
gen-gf-phudu-gf-palanquin: Phudu draws every letter with a flat, unvarying line and generous openings at the curve ends. And Palanquin counters with sans-serif curves whose mouths stay wide, so the two sit together with loud and level voices.
gen-gf-phudu-gf-philosopher: Philosopher reads clean and sure, with bowls that thin softly. Phudu, by contrast, holds one pen-like weight through every turn, which makes it a strong choice for large, brief headings.
gen-gf-phudu-gf-quattrocento-sans: Phudu builds each letter from a single monoline stroke, with open, generous curve endings that give it a bold, distinctive face. Quattrocento Sans sits beside it, modern and quiet.
gen-gf-phudu-gf-sansation: Phudu has a tube-like thickness that holds through every bend, and its curves finish in wide, generous openings. Sansation takes over beneath it, a friendly sans whose curves turn in without any ink pooling.
gen-gf-phudu-gf-shanti: Chunky, open, unmistakably loud. Phudu joins its strokes at full width with no hairline thinning, while Shanti brings a modern sans with a generous entry into the e's eye.
gen-gf-phudu-gf-snippet: Phudu keeps one pen-smooth line weight through every turn, its curves ending in wide openings that feel bold. Snippet is the wiry sans, with a crescent-wrench c.
gen-gf-phudu-gf-source-sans-3: Bold is the first word for Phudu, whose wire-like strokes stay constant and look best big and short. Source Sans 3 follows as a modern sans with an a whose lower bowl opens up.
gen-gf-phudu-gf-telex: Telex reads clean and loose, its curvy letters feeling unclamped. Phudu runs a single stroke width through the whole alphabet, which looks best big and short.
